scenario.symptoms: Push opt-out rate spiked 12% after a marketing campaign. Some users received 28 pushes in one day despite a product policy of max 3 ranked notifications per day.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Each vertical team runs its own ranker and sends directly to the delivery service. There is no global counter enforcing daily caps before send.

incident.headline: Multiple rankers bypass a global daily notification budget

agenda.goal: Enforce cross-channel notification budgets before delivery.
agenda.opener: Users got 28 pushes in a day—where should the daily cap be enforced in this stack?

evidence.strong: Central budget service with atomic counters, unified ranking gate, priority tiers, and defer/drop rules with audit logs.
evidence.weak: Trusts each ranker to self-limit sends.

misconceptions.pattern: Relying on client-side notification settings only.
misconceptions.challenge: How do you stop server-side marketing sends from ignoring the cap?

probes: How do you choose which notification wins when three teams compete for the last slot?
Where is the counter stored for idempotent retries?
hints: Think centralized gate vs many writers.
Redis INCR with TTL can track daily counts.
agenda.referenceFix: Route all sends through a budget-aware orchestrator that decrements per-user/day counters, applies priority rules, and drops or schedules overflow.

scenario.symptoms: Complaints flooded support after users in Europe received shopping alerts at 3 a.m. local time. The ranker schedules on UTC hour buckets using signup timezone only.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Users who traveled did not update profile timezone. The timing model uses a static table instead of recent device locale or IP hints.

incident.headline: Send-time model uses stale timezone so quiet hours fail

agenda.goal: Deliver ranked notifications in each user’s appropriate local window.
agenda.opener: Users got pushes at 3 a.m.—how should timing features decide when to send?

evidence.strong: Combines device-reported timezone, decaying travel signals, quiet-hour constraints, and per-user send windows in the ranker.
evidence.adequate: Uses profile timezone with manual update only.
evidence.weak: Schedules purely on UTC without user locale.

probes: What signal updates timezone when someone flies abroad?
How do you back off if the user dismisses late-night pushes?
hints: Mobile clients know local offset from the OS.
Quiet hours are a hard constraint, not just a model feature.
agenda.referenceFix: Ingest device timezone heartbeat, fall back to profile, enforce quiet-hour windows before scoring, and reschedule sends into the next allowed local slot.

nuggets.title: Same event ranked on push and email

scenario.symptoms: Users report duplicate alerts for the same order shipment on push, email, and SMS within two minutes. Engagement dropped because each channel ranker optimizes independently.
scenario.interviewerSetup: There is no dedupe key across channels. Each channel model scores the event separately and sends if above threshold.

incident.headline: Independent channel rankers triple-send the same logical notification

agenda.goal: Pick the best channel mix without spamming users for one event.
agenda.opener: Users got push, email, and SMS for one shipment—how would you coordinate ranking across channels?

evidence.strong: Unified decision layer with dedupe keys, channel preference model, mutual exclusion rules, and fallback only if primary undelivered.
evidence.adequate: Caps per channel but still allows triple send.

probes: When is it OK to use two channels for the same event?
How do you represent user channel preferences?
hints: Treat event+user as a single decision.
Delivery receipts can trigger fallback channel.
agenda.referenceFix: Central orchestrator scores channels jointly, sends at most one primary notification per dedupe key, and uses async fallback if delivery fails.
